paper_title: The Surprising Effectiveness of Deleting Weights in LLM Post-Training

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: How little of a pretrained large language model (LLM) has to change for it to acquire new capabilities? We find that zeroing fewer than 0.05% of its weights, with no other modification, matches full fine-tuning (FFT) at scale across three LLM post-training regimes: reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, supervised fine-tuning, and on-policy distillation. Our method, Deletion Tuning, learns a binary mask over the gate projection of transformer blocks. Two practical advantages follow: the trained mask is hundreds to thousands of times smaller than the corresponding FFT checkpoint, and Deletion Tuning forgets far less, which addresses a central challenge in continual learning. Under reinforcement learning, its prior-task accuracy stays near the base level while FFT, LoRA, and random sparse fine-tuning lose up to 5.4 points. To understand why masking alone suffices, we analyze the geometry of the learned weight changes under reinforcement learning using stable rank, spectrum drift, and principal-weight overlap. Compared with LoRA and random sparse fine-tuning, Deletion Tuning is closest to FFT across the three measures.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: To acquire new capabilities during LLM post-training, full fine-tuning can alter every parameter, LoRA (Hu et al., 2022) learns low-rank update, and the Multiple Ticket Hypothesis (MTH) (Adewuyi et al., 2026) and SHiRA (Bhardwaj et al., 2024) optimize values at selected weight positions. Weight deletion is typically used differently: pruning removes weights while preserving an already-trained models capabilities for efficient inference (Sun et al., 2024; Frantar and Alistarh, 2023), and the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis finds sparse subnetworks that can be trained to match dense networks (Frankle and Carbin, 2019). Unlike full fine-tuning, LoRA, and sparse updates, deletion writes no new values and only chooses which pretrained weights to keep. Recent work shows that fine-tuned solutions lie close to the pretrained model. RL fine-tuning changes only small subnetwork (Mukherjee et al., 2025), and task experts lie densely around pretrained weights (Gan and Isola, 2026). We push this observation to its limit across reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and on-policy distillation (OPD), and ask: Can pretrained LLM acquire new capabilities by learning only which weights to set to zero? The answer is yes across all three post-training regimes. We propose Deletion Tuning, which learns only binary mask over the gate-projection weights of transformer blocks. At deployment, each target weight * Equal contribution. Page 1 of 22 either retains its pretrained value or is set to zero, so the learned binary mask is the entire adapter. We test Deletion Tuning with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) (Shao et al., 2024) for RLVR, standard SFT, and Self-Distillation Fine-Tuning (SDFT) (Shenfeld et al., 2026a) for OPD. Our experiments span two model families, eight backbones from 0.5B to 30B, and both in-distribution and out-of-distribution evaluation. At the largest model scale tested in each setting, Deletion Tuning matches full fine-tuning (FFT) across reasoning, domain knowledge, and tool-use tasks. The binary-mask form brings two practical advantages: (i) the adapter is compact, with the trained mask hundreds to thousands of times smaller than the corresponding FFT checkpoint and smaller than even LoRA 𝑟=1 in our main GRPO comparison; and (ii) Deletion Tuning forgets less, with its forward KL remaining low and its prior-task accuracy staying near the base level across all three Llama scales. Under FFT, LoRA, and random sparse fine-tuning, forward KL grows and prior-task accuracy falls (Figure 2), consistent with forward KL as predictor of forgetting (Shenfeld et al., 2026b). Learning new tasks while keeping old ones makes Deletion Tuning promising candidate for continual learning. Finally, we examine why Deletion Tuning can match FFT with deletion alone. We confirm that the gains come from learning the mask rather than the Wanda prior used in its initialization. We also find that the geometry of Deletion Tunings learned weight updates tracks FFTs more closely than LoRA or random sparse fine-tuning across stable rank, spectrum drift, and principal-weight overlap. Our contributions are as follows: Deletion alone matches FFT. Deletion Tuning learns which gate-projection weights to delete (Section 4). It is on par with FFT at the largest scale we test in GRPO, SFT, and SDFT, up to 30B mixture-of-experts model (Sections 5.2 and 5.6). Under GRPO, it also solves problems that the base model fails in all 128 sampled attempts (Section 5.2). Deletion Tuning is compact and forgets less. Its masks are orders of magnitude smaller than FFT checkpoints in all three regimes (Sections 5.2 and 5.6), and it keeps prior-task accuracy throughout training (Section 5.4). Deletion Tunings learned updates have FFT-like geometry.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: LLM post-training. We study three post-training regimes that differ in where the training signal comes from. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) imitates fixed labeled targets (Wei et al., 2022; Ouyang et al., 2022; Taori et al., 2023). Reinforcement learning optimizes reward on the models own samples, from PPO-based RLHF (Schulman et al., 2017; Ouyang et al., 2022) to GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) with verifiable rewards, the recipe behind DeepSeek-R1 (Guo et al., 2025a). With verifiable rewards, rule-based checkers or LLM verifiers score each sample (Lu et al., 2026a). DPO (Rafailov et al., 2023) instead turns preferences into closed-form loss. On-policy distillation trains student on its own rollouts to match teachers per-token distribution (Agarwal et al., 2024; Shenfeld et al., 2026a; Zhao et al., 2026), and SDFT uses it to reduce catastrophic forgetting (Kirkpatrick et al., 2017). Self-distillation can also teach reasoning behaviors (Sprague et al., 2026). We use all three to test whether deletion works as general post-training mechanism. Sparsity and selective parameter updates. One-shot LLM pruning methods like Wanda (Sun et al., 2024) and SparseGPT (Frantar and Alistarh, 2023) extend classical magnitude-based pruning (Han et al., 2015; Zhu and Gupta, 2018) to LLM scale, while continuous relaxations (Louizos et al., 2018; Maddison et al., 2017; Jang et al., 2017) make binary masks differentiable. Unstructured pruning can even retain Page 2 of 22 Figure 1: Deletion Tuning learns which pretrained weights to delete and writes no new values. The pretrained weights 𝑊 stay frozen, and each is paired with trainable logit in 𝐺, the only parameters that post-training updates. During training, each weight is multiplied by 𝜎(𝛼𝐺), smooth mask between 0 and 1. The sharpness 𝛼 rises over training until the sigmoid becomes hard threshold at 𝐺 = 0. At deployment, weights with positive logits (blue) keep their pretrained values and weights with negative logits (red) are set to zero (crossed out), so the trained adapter is one bit per weight. the test-time scaling of reasoning models (Monjur et al., 2026). Earlier mask learning adapted vision backbones and encoder-only language models to downstream tasks such as image and sentence classification (Mallya et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2020; Radiya-Dixit and Wang, 2020). Recent mask methods target semi-structured LLM inference sparsity (Fang et al., 2024), refinement of fine-tuned LLM (Zhang et al., 2025), or vision-language backbones (Zheng et al., 2023). Deletion Tuning instead makes the mask the entire post-training update of pretrained LLM across RLVR, SFT, and OPD, and it learns how many weights to delete. Sparse weight tuning writes float deltas at selected positions (Guo et al., 2021; Sung et al., 2021; Adewuyi et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2025; Bhardwaj et al., 2024), additive adapters introduce trainable float parameters (Hu et al., 2022; Morris et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2025; Houlsby et al., 2019; Lester et al., 2021; Lu et al., 2026b), and robust fine-tuning methods restrict or regularize movement of pretrained weights under distribution shift (Lee et al., 2023; Tian et al., 2024). Deletion Tuning instead keeps every retained weight at its pretrained value and learns only which gate-projection weights to delete. Understanding LLM fine-tuning. The classical Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (Frankle and Carbin, 2019) posits that randomly initialized networks contain sparse subnetworks that train to comparable accuracy in isolation. Recent work characterizes pretrained-model fine-tuning along three axes. Density: task-expert solutions densely populate the neighborhood of pretrained weights (Gan and Isola, 2026). Geometry: Mukherjee et al. (2025) report that RL fine-tuning naturally updates only 5 to 30% of parameters across PPO, GRPO, DPO, and several model families. Zhu et al. (2026) show these updates land off the principal weights of 𝑊0 while leaving the spectrum largely intact, where principal weights are the top-magnitude entries of the rank-𝑘 SVD reconstruction of 𝑊0 (Liu et al., 2025). Forgetting: Shenfeld et al. (2026b) establish that the forward KL between fine-tuned and base policies on the new task accurately predicts forgetting. Deletion Tuning reproduces the off-principal update pattern and low spectrum drift. Deletion Tunings low forward KL also predicts the strong prior-task retention we measure (Section 5.4).

sections.title: 4 Deletion Tuning
sections.content: Deletion Tuning parameterizes fine-tuning as one trainable scalar logit per pretrained weight at chosen subset of linear layers, with the base model frozen. During training, sigmoid of each logit is annealed toward step function, and at deployment each logit becomes single bit deciding whether the corresponding weight is kept or deleted (set to zero). In pruning terms, Deletion Tuning performs learned unstructured pruning to fine-tune the model. Notation. Let 𝑊 ℝ𝑑out𝑑in denote target weight matrix in the pretrained model and 𝐺 ℝ𝑑out𝑑in trainable logit matrix of the same shape, where the sign of 𝐺𝑖𝑗 at deployment decides whether 𝑊𝑖𝑗 is kept (positive) or zeroed (negative). sections.title: 5.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: Tasks, benchmarks, and models. We study three post-training regimes on two model families, referring to family as Llama or Qwen and to size by its suffix (e.g., Llama1B, Qwen7B). Evaluation uses greedy decoding, and we report the best validation accuracy across saved checkpoints. GRPO, in distribution. We train and evaluate on GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021) with Llama1B, Llama3B, and Llama8B (Llama3.2-1B/3B-Instruct and Llama3-8B-Instruct) (Llama Team, AI @ Meta, 2024), validating every 25 optimizer steps. GRPO, out of distribution. Following SimpleRL-Zoo (Zeng et al., 2025), we train on its math corpus and report the mean over six held-out benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH500, Minerva Math, OlympiadBench, AIME24, AMC23; per-benchmark results in Appendix C) with Qwen0.5B, Qwen3B, and Qwen7B (Qwen2.5 base) (Qwen Team, 2024). At larger scale, we add Qwen14B (Qwen2.514B) and the Qwen3-30B-A3B mixture-of-experts model (30B total and 3B active parameters). We validate every 10 optimizer steps. SFT. We train Llama1B and Llama3B (Llama3.2-1B/3B-Instruct) separately on each of the 14 MMLUPro (Wang et al., 2024) subjects and 23 BBEH (Kazemi et al., 2025) subtasks, validate at the end of training, and average accuracy within each suite. SDFT. We follow the ToolAlpaca (Tang et al., 2023) tool-use and Science settings of Shenfeld et al. (2026a) with Qwen7B (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct), reporting exact-match accuracy under each tasks evaluator. Science is the Chemistry L-3 subset of SciKnowEval (Feng et al., 2024). We validate every 100 optimizer steps on ToolAlpaca and every 25 on Science. Training pipelines. All runs use AdamW with fp32 master weights, bf16 mixed precision, and gradient checkpointing. GRPO. We use verl (Sheng et al., 2025) with constant learning rate. GSM8K uses prompt batch 64, 𝑛=4 rollouts, response length 4096, 3 epochs, and no KL penalty, while SimpleRL-Zoo uses prompt batch 256, 𝑛=8 rollouts, response length 4096, 150 steps, and KL penalty 104. SFT. We minimize cross-entropy with constant learning rate for 𝑇 =400 steps per task at effective batch 4, with 75/25 train/eval split (per-task counts in Appendix D). SDFT. We follow Shenfeld et al. (2026a): cosine schedule with 0.1 warmup ratio, prompt batch 32, 2 epochs, EMA mixup 𝛾 = 0.01, and one demonstration prepended to the teachers input. Baselines. All three baselines use the same data and number of steps as Deletion Tuning. FFT. Full fine-tuning trains all weights and is the reference we aim to match. Its learning rate is 106 on GSM8K, 5107 on SimpleRL-Zoo, 106 to 3106 on SFT (Appendix H), and 5105 on SDFT as in Shenfeld et al. (2026a). The same restriction pays off more clearly for retention, where Deletion Tuning keeps the prior-task accuracy that FFT loses (Section 5.4). The gap to FFT closes with scale. At smaller backbones, Deletion Tuning recovers 90% to 99% of FFTs accuracy. At larger scale, Deletion Tuning matches FFT on Qwen14B and on the Qwen3-30B-A3B mixture-of-experts model  (Table 2)  . sections.title: 5.3 Learning the Mask Drives the Gains
sections.content: Do Deletion Tunings gains over the base model come from learning the mask itself, beyond the Wanda prior that initializes the gates? We test this directly. For each run in Table 1, we apply Wanda one-shot pruning without GRPO training at 8 sparsity levels from 1/2 to 1/8192. We evaluate each level on the same validation set and record the best accuracy (Appendix reports every level). Table 4 compares this best-Wanda score with the base model and the trained Deletion Tuning mask. The best Wanda mask stays within 2.4 points of the base on all six backbones, while Deletion Tuning, starting from the same Wanda scores, gains up to 53.2 points.

sections.title: 5.4 Deletion Tuning Forgets Less
sections.content: Forward KL on the new task predicts how much fine-tuned model forgets (Shenfeld et al., 2026b). We hypothesize that deletion keeps the perturbation to the base policy small, because each edit can only set weight to zero and training chooses which few weights to edit, yielding low forward KL and therefore little forgetting. Following Shenfeld et al. (2026b)s evaluation, Figure 2 tracks forward KL and prior-task accuracy over training for FFT, LoRA, MTH, and Deletion Tuning at the three Llama scales. The prior-task suite has six benchmarks: HellaSwag, MMLU, TruthfulQA, WinoGrande, IFEval, and HumanEval. By step 348, FFTs forward KL reaches 1.0 on Llama1B and 1.5 on Llama8B, and its prior-task accuracy ends 1.3 to 3.1 points below base. Deletion Tunings forward KL stays at or below 0.05 at all three scales, and its prior-task accuracy stays within one point of base throughout training. LoRA and MTH train only small fraction of parameters, yet their forward KL reaches 0.4 to 1.3 and their prior-task accuracy falls up to 5.4 points below base. MTH at 99.95% sparsity trains 0.05% of all parameters, comparable to the 0.035% to 0.046% that Deletion Tuning deletes at these scales  (Table 7)  , suggesting that the small number of edited weights does not explain Deletion Tunings retention, and that deletion itself keeps forgetting low.

sections.title: 5.6 Generalizing Beyond GRPO: Results on SFT and SDFT
sections.content: Does deletion also work when the training signal is denser or comes from outside the model? GRPO samples from the model itself and rewards whole responses, and RL updates of this kind are known to be sparse (Mukherjee et al., 2025). SFT instead imitates fixed external targets token by token and produces dense updates (Mukherjee et al., 2025), which makes it harder test for an adapter that can only delete. SDFT sits in between: the student samples its own responses, and teacher supplies target distribution at every token. We test Deletion Tuning with SFT on knowledge and reasoning benchmarks (MMLU-Pro and BBEH) and with SDFT on tool use (ToolAlpaca) and science questions (Science), using the setups of Section 5.1. Under SFT, Deletion Tuning matches FFT at 3B on both MMLU-Pro and BBEH  (Table 5)  . Under SDFT, Deletion Tuning matches FFT on both Qwen7B tasks  (Table 6)  . In both regimes, its adapters are 600 to 4,700 smaller than FFT checkpoints.

sections.title: 5.7 Deletion Tuning Is Robust to Hyperparameter Changes
sections.content: Deletion Tuning works across range of values for its hyperparameters: initial sparsity 𝜂, learning rate lr, and sparse-weight regularization strength 𝜆. We sweep 𝜂 {1/2048, 1/4096, 1/8192}, lr {104, 3104}, and 𝜆 {0, 105} on Llama8B GSM8K and Qwen7B SimpleRL-Zoo (Tables 13 and 14 in Appendix G). Every setting lands within 1.6 points of the best run on Llama8B and within 3.2 points on Qwen7B, and the single configuration we use for all main runs is at or near the best setting at both backbones. sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduced Deletion Tuning, which fine-tunes model by learning only binary mask over its gate projections. At the largest scale we test in each regime (Qwen14B and the Qwen3-30B-A3B mixture-of-experts model under GRPO, Qwen7B under SDFT, and Llama3B under SFT), it matches full fine-tuning. The mask is smaller than rank-1 LoRA and hundreds to thousands of times smaller than an FFT checkpoint. In our GRPO retention runs, Deletion Tuning keeps prior-task accuracy near the base level throughout training, while FFT, LoRA, and MTH lose up to 5.4 points. Its weight updates also resemble FFTs more closely than those of LoRA or MTH across stable rank, spectrum drift, and principal-weight overlap, which helps explain how deletion alone can match FFT. These results suggest that post-training can work by selection alone, keeping nearly every pretrained weight and choosing the few to delete. Limitations and Future Work. Because Deletion Tuning forgets little, natural next test is continual learning over sequence of tasks. Training keeps one logit per masked weight, so Deletion Tuning uses less training memory than FFT but more than LoRA. Restricting the logits to small set of candidate weights could close this gap. The masks are also small and discrete, which aids interpretability: comparing which weights different tasks delete could localize the changes that post-training makes to model. Masks for different tasks might also be combined, for example by taking their union, to merge skills without further training. Finally, restricting the mask to 𝑁 𝑀, channel-wise, or block patterns could let one mask both adapt and compress the model. Page 12 of

sections.title: F Algebraic Connection to MaskLLM
sections.content: Deletion Tuning and MaskLLM (Fang et al., 2024) arrive at their forward passes from different starting points: Deletion Tuning from continuous relaxation of per-weight binary masking decision (Eq. The base weight matrix is partitioned into groups of 𝑀 contiguous weights, and each group is handled independently.
